Space reactors require reliable heat rejection without pumps, and sodium heat pipes offer a passive solution whose behaviour in microgravity is difficult to predict without a validated model. This study develops a one-dimensional reduced-order model of two-phase flow that solves compressible vapour momentum, Darcy filtration, five operating limits, and a thermal resistance network, and applies it to the 500 kWth *Indonesian Space Reactor* (ISR) core containing 61 uranium nitride pins.

The model is verified by grid convergence, energy balance, and analytical comparison, and validated against five steady-state conditions of the KRUSTY test using two calibrated interfacial constants and a leave-one-out protocol (MAPE 4.68%; $R^2 = 0.961$). At the 1075 K design point the limiting mechanism is entrainment (15.22 kW), not the capillary limit (51.97 kW), and an 18 mm pipe is selected with a safety factor of 1.37.

All 61 pins can be cooled passively with a peak fuel temperature of 1249 K. Eliminating the Na-78K pump loop removes 40.94 kg of subsystem mass (63.0%) and 0.53 kW of parasitic power, but requires 27.2% fuel volume, reducing core life from 17 to 12.4 years. The principal benefit is inherent safety rather than mass saving.
